topic: Door latch: why does a door click shut by itself? (the spring latch bolt's slanted side is pushed in by the strike plate, the spring snaps it into the strike hole, the flat side holds the door, the handle pulls it back).
principle: The spring-loaded latch bolt has a slanted side facing the closing direction: when the door closes, the strike plate's edge pushes on the slant and drives the bolt into the door against its spring; at the strike hole the spring snaps the bolt out; pulling the door presses the bolt's flat side against the hole's edge, which pushes sideways and cannot drive it in, so the door holds until the handle retracts the bolt.
caption:
Why does a door click shut by itself? 🚪
Guess: which side holds it, slanted or flat? 👇

firstComment:
Answer: the flat side 🔧

The latch bolt in the door's edge is spring-loaded and has one slanted side, facing the way the door closes.

Close the door: the slanted side hits the strike plate on the frame, which pushes the bolt into the door and squeezes its spring.

When the bolt reaches the hole in the strike plate, the spring snaps it out. That's the click.

Now pull the door: the flat side presses against the edge of the hole. It pushes sideways, not inward, so the bolt stays out and the door stays shut.

Turn the handle and it pulls the bolt back into the door, so the door can open.

(Simplified 3D model, slowed down. The parts that link the handle to the bolt are hidden in the dark box, and the sizes are approximate.)

Sources:
Wikipedia, Latch (a latch bolt is a spring-loaded bolt with an angled edge; when the door is pushed closed, the angled edge engages the lip of the strike plate and the spring allows the bolt to retract; once the door is fully closed, the bolt extends into the strike plate, holding the door closed; turning the handle retracts it): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latch
US patent 4,854,618 (a spring-loaded latch bolt with a slanted contact face on one side and a surface parallel to the door's edge on the other; the slanted face must face the direction the door moves to close; slammed shut, the slanted face meets the striker plate, the bolt retracts and then springs out into the strike opening): https://patents.justia.com/patent/4854618
Inspire Hardware, Door Latch Parts (as the door closes, the bevel meets the strike and pushes the bolt inward; once the bolt reaches the opening, its spring lets it extend into the frame; turning the knob or lever retracts it): https://www.inspirehardware.com/blogs/news/door-latch-parts-terminology
altText: 3D animation of a door latch. A white door with a silver lever handle swings toward a gray door frame; a brass latch bolt with one slanted side sticks out of the door's edge, and a silver strike plate with a hole sits on the frame. The top is cut away to show the inside from above: the bolt slides in a tube with a coil spring behind it. As the door closes, the strike plate pushes on the bolt's slanted side and the bolt slides into the door, squeezing the spring. At the hole the spring snaps the bolt out with a click and the door stops against the frame. When the door is pulled, the bolt's flat side presses on the edge of the hole and the door stays shut. Then the handle turns, the bolt slides back in and the door swings open. Text on screen: Why does it click? Slant gets pushed in. Click! A spring snaps it in. Flat side holds. Handle pulls it back.
